## Conflict Communications Paper

Disagreements often start small and quickly turn personal. A comment about a child’s diet can feel like a challenge to competence. Employee pushback can shift into a power struggle. Even unfinished work can become more about blame than about getting the tasks done. Three layers of brain function—automatic, social and emotional, and deliberate—influence what we notice in a conflict and how we respond (Miller, 2015).

The lizard brain is instinctive and habitual. It is focused on survival and reacts quickly, often before we have time to think. It also relies on habits, training, rituals, and familiar patterns. If a response got us through a situation before, the lizard brain treats that as evidence the same response will work again, even when the circumstances have changed. In conflict, the lizard brain can automatically shut down, snap back, become defensive, avoid the situation, or fall into an old pattern without first deciding whether the response makes sense. The same automatic system can also protect us by noticing potential danger before we have consciously identified what is making us uncomfortable (Miller, 2015).

I experienced the protective side of the lizard brain in my early twenties while backing out of my driveway in Florida. A woman I did not know approached my car and asked if I could give her a ride home because she was having cramps. I was conflicted because my first reaction was to help. As she spoke, several details did not make sense. It was around 90 degrees outside, yet she was wearing a full sweatsuit to work out. She did not have a cell phone, and when I asked where she needed to go, the area she mentioned was not residential. None of those details proved she was dangerous, but together they made me concerned enough that I was not willing to let her into my car.

I told her I was uncomfortable giving a ride to someone I did not know, but I could call a patrol car to help her. I later learned emergency services had received reports of similar suspicious incidents in the area. I never learned whether the woman actually posed a threat, and I never saw her walking in my neighborhood again. I only knew the details did not make sense, and I could not justify the risk of driving someone I did not know to an unfamiliar location. My automatic reaction did not stop me from helping; it changed how I helped. I called someone who could help without leaving me alone in a car with a stranger. I would make the same decision today.

The monkey brain is social and emotional. It cares about belonging, connection, hierarchy, status, and how other people see us. The monkey brain wants to know where we fit in the group, where we stand in relation to others, and what other people think of us—even when what we think they believe may not be true. It prefers clear roles and familiar group norms because they make our place in the group easier to understand. The monkey brain can also resist change when a new person, idea, or way of doing something threatens status, identity, tradition, or the way the group operates. Once emotion takes over, solving the actual problem can become less important than protecting ourselves, our position in the group, or our side (Miller, 2015).

I experienced the defensive side of the monkey brain when a recent comment from my husband felt like a challenge to my competence. He said Gentry, our son, needed to eat more protein. On the surface, he was talking about our son’s diet. I am his mother; I manage most of what he eats, and I have an undergraduate degree in Food Science and Human Nutrition and am a registered dietitian. I did not hear, *Is Gentry getting enough protein?* I heard, *You are not feeding him right.*

I immediately became defensive. I explained what Gentry eats and why his protein intake was not a concern. I had the professional knowledge to support what I was saying, but I was no longer using my knowledge to address his concern. I was defending my competence as both his mother and a dietitian. The more I defended myself, the more defensive my husband became. He eventually apologized and said he had only been making a comment. I told him I was not discussing it anymore.

We never answered the question that started the disagreement. If my husband’s concern was whether Gentry was getting enough protein, we could have tracked what he ate for a few days and calculated his intake. Instead, I treated his comment as a judgment of my competence. My husband then defended what he meant, while I defended why I was right. More nutrition evidence would not have fixed the conversation because we were no longer having a nutrition discussion.

I would handle this situation differently now, though I would not pretend to have no emotional reaction. I might still think, *Really? Are you questioning me about protein?* Instead of immediately defending myself, I could ask what concerned my husband. We could then look at what Gentry was actually eating. If his protein intake was low, we would know we had something to address. If his intake was adequate, we would have answered the original question without turning the conversation into an argument about my competence. My husband commented on Gentry’s protein intake; I turned the comment into a criticism of my competence.

The human brain is thoughtful and deliberate. It is slower than the lizard and monkey brains because it gathers information, thinks through what is happening, and decides what problem needs solving before choosing a response. The goal is to solve the problem, not win a status contest. Because automatic and emotional reactions happen faster, the human brain is often playing catch-up. Using the human brain does not mean having no emotion. It means noticing the emotion and choosing what to do next, rather than letting the emotion make that choice. The human brain can also recognize when a familiar script is running and decide whether to stay with it, switch roles, or stop the script altogether (Miller, 2015).

I experienced the value of choosing a deliberate response earlier in my career when an employee challenged my authority. I was a young dietitian and the new program director for a hospital weight-management program. One of the exercise physiologists in the wellness center did not want to work with me. He had more experience than I did and thought he should have been put in charge of the program.

I could have gone over his head and asked our boss to intervene, but involving our boss likely would have kept the monkey dance going. Instead, I got creative. I went to the front desk and scheduled an hour of training with him just as any other client would.

I used the hour to build rapport. I let him teach me, asked about his experience, and looked for common ground. I never mentioned my position or the fact that he had refused to work with me. At the end of the hour, I told him, “You know so much about this. I could use your help with the weight-management program.” I was asking for his expertise, not telling him he had to work for me.

After that meeting, he started coming to my office with ideas. He became involved in the weight-management program, and eventually we were helping each other with projects throughout the wellness center. Going over his head might have forced him to work with me, but it probably would not have made him want to. By asking for his expertise rather than using my position to force cooperation, I broke the script that had kept us in a power struggle (Miller, 2015). Not every challenge to a leader’s authority requires the leader to demonstrate authority.

Years later, when I owned L. Mae Boutique, our flagship store and warehouse were in the middle of moving to a new location, and I had just returned from a buying trip at market. I had been traveling and working 12-hour days, I was pregnant, and I was carrying the stress of the move on top of running the business. When I returned to our offices after the trip, boxes of new merchandise were still sitting unprocessed in the warehouse. Until we processed the merchandise, we could not photograph it, enter it into inventory, send it to stores, or sell it.

I then overheard the warehouse manager and two employees socializing while the boxes sat there. I watched them on the camera system for about 20 minutes and became increasingly angry. When I finally confronted them, I raised my voice, they became defensive, and the conversation escalated.

The unfinished work was a legitimate performance problem, but I was also tired, stressed, pregnant, and already frustrated. I was much more susceptible to taking a hook than I would have been under normal circumstances. A hook provides the excuse or permission for behavior we are already motivated to engage in (Miller, 2015). All three employees had been having performance issues before that morning, so I was not reacting only to the boxes sitting in the warehouse. I was also reacting to accumulated frustration with their prior performance problems. Seeing them socialize while pressing work remained unfinished gave that frustration somewhere to go. I took the hook, they became defensive, and their defensiveness made me angrier. The conversation became a monkey dance instead of a discussion about why the merchandise had not been processed.

The next day, I apologized to each woman individually and had a much more productive conversation. I asked what had prevented the boxes from being processed and what I could do to help remove those barriers. We also talked about how employees could build relationships without letting gossip and socializing interfere with pressing work.

I should have handled those first 20 minutes differently. Rather than watching the employees on camera and getting progressively angrier, I could have walked into the back office, briefly joined their conversation, and then met with each woman individually to review her tasks for the day and week. I could have checked what was getting done, what was falling behind, and whether anyone needed help getting back on track.

The following day, I still would have had individual conversations about why the merchandise was sitting unprocessed and how much time was being spent socializing. The difference is that I would not have been trying to repair the damage from losing my temper the day before. We could have addressed the performance issues without everyone coming into the conversation already defensive.

I also waited too long to address some performance problems because I did not want to micromanage. I intentionally gave my managers responsibilities, timelines, and goals while allowing them considerable freedom in how they managed their work. I still believe in that approach, but autonomy requires personal responsibility. Clear boundaries are not micromanagement; employees can have discretion in how they approach their work while still being held accountable when performance falls short of expectations.

Two of the employees involved in this conflict were people I should have removed from the business sooner. I kept trying to coach, redirect, and give additional chances even as their behavior negatively affected the team. A leader’s desire to keep a group together can make it harder to address toxic behavior, even when the damage to the team is clear (Miller, 2015).

At the same time, leaders need to be careful not to mistake disagreement for disrespect. Being in charge does not make someone immune to taking a hook or getting caught up in a monkey dance (Miller, 2015). When a leader reacts defensively, an ordinary disagreement can become a performance issue that affects an employee’s job. Before responding, a leader should consider whether the employee is genuinely challenging their authority or simply expressing a different opinion. A legitimate performance or conduct problem may require accountability; disagreement with a decision may simply require listening.

An employee may resist a decision because it reduces their influence, overlooks their experience, or changes a familiar way of working. Repeating the rationale for the decision will not necessarily address those concerns (Miller, 2015). With the exercise physiologist, recognizing his expertise turned resistance into participation. With the warehouse employees, asking why the work was unfinished would have given me the information I needed to decide whether the problem required support, clearer expectations, or consequences.

Authority also does not require control over every decision an employee makes. Being led requires more personal responsibility than being managed, because employees must exercise judgment rather than rely on a rule for every situation (Miller, 2015). Leaders need enough structure for employees to understand the standard, but not so many rules that following the rule becomes a substitute for judgment. Listening and understanding help leaders make better decisions; they do not eliminate the need to set expectations, address poor performance, or remove someone who repeatedly damages the team.

The goal is not to eliminate conflict or prevent lizard and monkey reactions. It is to recognize when status, emotion, habit, or group loyalty has replaced figuring out what happened, what needs to change, and who is responsible for changing it. In practice, leaders need to recognize their own reactions, identify the hook or script, and listen long enough to understand what the other person is defending or objecting to. From there, they can look for common ground, choose how to respond, and notice whether the conversation is becoming more productive or more defensive. Continuing to push the same approach when someone becomes increasingly defensive is unlikely to help, even when the leader believes the decision is right. A leader can listen without agreeing, reduce defensiveness without lowering the standard, and give employees autonomy while still holding them accountable for results.

## References

Miller, R. (2015). *Conflict communication: A new paradigm in conscious communication*. YMAA Publication Center.
